notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 112, drawn from the traditional commentators and denominational sources I was able to access.

---

## Overview

Psalm 112 is an acrostic psalm (22 lines, each beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet), a deliberate twin to Psalm 111. Spurgeon wrote: “It bears the same relation to the preceding which the moon does to the sun; for, while the first declares the glory of God, the second speaks of the reflection of the divine brightness in men born from above.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm) Both Boice and Hengstenberg stress this pairing: Psalm 111 celebrates God's character and works; Psalm 112 describes the godly person who reflects God's own attributes. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/psalms-112.html)

---

## Verse 1

**"Hallelujah! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments."**

The psalm opens with "Hallelujah" (Praise the LORD), which Spurgeon notes is both the psalmist's personal praise and an exhortation to all who observe the godly life: “The Psalm cannot be viewed as the extolling of man, for it commences with 'Praise ye the Lord;' and it is intended to give to God all the honour of his grace which is manifested in the sons of God.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

This verse picks up directly from Psalm 111:10, where the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The blessed man's fear is not servile terror but “profound reverence” and awe (Boice, cited in Guzik). Gill makes the same distinction: the fear is “not with a servile, but with a godly fear” — a reverence for God's goodness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

The second half of the verse balances fear with delight. As Boice observed, Psalm 111:2 spoke of delight in God's *works*, while Psalm 112:1 speaks of delight in God's *words* (commands). Kidner adds: “To this man God's word is as fascinating as are his works to the naturalist; and the term used for it, his commandments, implies that his interest is practical.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/) Spurgeon stresses that “cheerful obedience is the only acceptable obedience; he who obeys reluctantly is disobedient at heart.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Horne adds a memorable summary: “The man who duly 'feareth God,' is delivered from every other fear; the man who 'delighteth in God's commandments,' is freed from every inordinate desire of earthly things.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

---

## Verse 2

**"His descendants will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed."**

Ellicott notes that “mighty” here is in the sense of *wealthy* or *prosperous*, as in Ruth 2:1 (the same Hebrew phrase *gibbor chayil* used of Boaz). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm) The Pulpit Commentary agrees, citing the use of the phrase in Ruth 2:1 and 1 Samuel 9:1 to mean “wealthy, prosperous.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon cautions that this promise is “a general statement rather than a promise made to every individual, for the children of the godly are not all prosperous, nor all famous.” Yet he maintains that “he who fears God, and leads a holy life, is, as a rule, doing the best he can for the future advancement of his house; no inheritance is equal to that of an unblemished name.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Gill extends the application to spiritual descendants, comparing believers as “the seed of Abraham” through faith. He also sees a reference to the “spiritual seed of Christ,” making Christ Himself the ultimate “man” who feared the LORD. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

---

## Verse 3

**"Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever."**

Spurgeon is notably cautious here: “Understood literally this is rather a promise of the old covenant than of the new, for many of the best of the people of God are very poor; yet it has been found true that uprightness is the road to success, and, all other things being equal, the honest man is the rising man.” He adds a spiritual reading: “What wealth can equal that of the love of God? What riches can rival a contented heart?” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Barnes (cited by Spurgeon/Guzik) reinforces the general-rule understanding: “Such promises are expected to be fulfilled in general; it is not required by any proper rules of interpreting language that this should be universally and always true.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

The Pulpit Commentary invokes Bishop Butler's *Analogy*: in God's moral government of the world, “virtue tends to accumulate to itself the good things of this life, and vice to disperse and dissipate them.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

The phrase **“his righteousness endures forever”** draws particular attention. Gill sees three possible meanings: (1) his inherent righteousness as a new creation in Christ that continues; (2) the imputed righteousness of Christ, which is everlasting; (3) his liberality/alms-giving (since *righteousness* can mean almsgiving in Hebrew usage). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm) Ellicott, citing the Talmud and Daniel 4:27 (LXX), favors the third sense here: that “righteousness” means *liberality or beneficence*. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** The Ligonier devotional on Psalm 112 stresses that v.6's promise about never being moved “does not mean righteous men and women never face hardship but that they persevere and are never finally crushed by their trouble.” Calvin is quoted: the righteous “are indeed liable to the incidents common to humanity… but their confidence remains unshaken, and by invincible patience they surmount all their adversities.” The devotional also insists that “the kind of righteousness to which the psalmist refers is primarily the imperfect, practical righteousness that is the fruit of our sanctification, but we must also see here an allusion to the perfect righteousness of Christ that we receive in our justification.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/unmovable-righteous)

---

## Verse 4

**"Light dawns in the darkness for the upright — for the gracious, compassionate, and righteous."**

The Hebrew verb for “arises/dawns” is commonly used of sunrise (Ellicott). “For the good man the darkest night of trouble and sorrow will have a dawn of hope.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

Delitzsch (cited in Guzik): “God himself is the light which arises in darkness for those who are sincere in their dealings with him.” Boice develops the sun-moon image: as the moon reflects the sun's light, so the godly reflect God's own character. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

The second half of the verse is debated: does it describe God or the upright man? The Pulpit Commentary insists the entire subject of the psalm is “the righteous, God-like man,” so the adjectives describe *him*: “In him are reflected shadows of all the Divine qualities.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm) Ellicott agrees: the Authorised Version is “right in making this a description of the upright man's character.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm) Gill presents both views but leans toward it being about God — because God is gracious and compassionate, “therefore he causes light to arise to them in darkness.” The Arabic and Ethiopic versions take this reading. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon reconciles the two: “This is spoken of God in the fourth verse of the hundred and eleventh Psalm, and now the same words are used of his servant: thus we are taught that when God makes a man upright, he makes him like himself.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Hengstenberg (Lutheran/Reformed) reads v.4 as describing the upright man: “There ariseth in darkness light to the upright, who is gracious and compassionate and just.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/psalms-112.html)

VanGemeren (cited in Guzik) notes that “the psalm gives a realistic portrayal of wisdom as it brings out, not only the blessings of honor, children, and riches, but also the reality of adversities.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

---

## Verse 5

**"It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice."**

Ellicott translates: “Happy is the man who gives and lends” — the word “good” here means *prosperous* or *fortunate* rather than morally good. He also reads the Hebrew for “guide his affairs” as “he will gain his cause in (the) judgment,” suggesting a legal setting where the righteous man is vindicated. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary sees the verse as “exegetical of the latter clause of v.4,” showing how the righteous man's compassion works: he shows favour and lends to the needy (referencing Deuteronomy 15:8, 11). The phrase “with discretion” is better rendered “with equity.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon gives a practical portrait: “Providence has made him able to lend, and grace makes him willing to lend. He is not a borrower, for God has lifted him above that necessity; neither is he a hoarder, for his new nature saves him from that temptation.” On guiding affairs with discretion, he adds: “True religion is sanctified common sense. Attention to the things of heaven does not necessitate the neglect of the affairs of earth.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Kidner's structural observation: Psalm 112:3 referred to wealth; vv.4–8 now “deal realistically with the temptations that go with the possession of money” — abuse of power, refusing to lend, fear, rivalry, and lack of generosity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

Poole (cited in Guzik): The man guides his affairs “with judgment; so as is fit and meet, and as God requires, not getting his estate unjustly, nor casting it away prodigally or wickedly, nor yet withholding it uncharitably from such as need it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

---

## Verse 6

**"Surely he will never be shaken; the righteous man will be remembered forever."**

The Pulpit Commentary emphasizes stability as a necessary element of happiness: “God's blessing shall abide with him, and make his happiness sure and stable.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon enumerates the dimensions of this stability: prosperity that is permanent (unlike the gambler's or cheat's), reputation that is bright and lustrous from year to year, a home that is permanent, and a memory that is abiding. “The righteous are worth remembering, their actions are of the kind which record themselves, and God himself takes charge of their memorials.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Maclaren (cited by Guzik): “He who builds his transient life on and into the Rock of Ages wins rocklike steadfastness…. Lives rooted in God are never uprooted.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

Gill reads this through a Calvinistic lens of perseverance: the righteous man “shall not be moved for ever… out of the heart of God, and from his love and affections; out of the covenant of grace… out of the hands of Christ, or off of him the foundation.” Though he may be shaken by afflictions or even “fall from some degree of steadfastness in the faith, and into sin, yet not so as to perish everlastingly: the saint's perseverance is a sure and certain truth, and to be depended upon.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

---

## Verse 7

**"He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD."**

Ellicott points to Job as the great illustration: “The story of Job, when the messengers of ill succeeded one another so fast, is an illustration of the truth of this verse.” He quotes Shakespeare's *Measure for Measure*: “Virtue is bold, and goodness never fearful.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “Confident in God's goodness towards him, he will not anticipate misfortunes. They may come… but he will not meet them half-way. His heart is fixed; i.e. firmly established — settled on a sure basis — trusting in the Lord — the one basis that is solid and immovable.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon: “He shall have no dread that evil tidings will come, and he shall not be alarmed when they do come. Rumours and reports he despises; prophecies of evil, vented by fanatical mouths, he ridicules; actual and verified information of loss and distress he bears with equanimity, resigning everything into the hands of God.” He adds: “He is neither fickle nor cowardly; when he is undecided as to his course he is still fixed in heart: he may change his plan, but not the purpose of his soul.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

F.B. Meyer (cited in Guzik): “There cannot be evil tidings to the soul which has fixed its trust in the Lord…. If tidings were to come to you today of disease, loss, bereavement, death, they could not be evil if your heart dares to maintain a fixed trust in God; for such trust robs death of its sting, and the grave of its victory. I cannot understand, but I can trust Him.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

**Baptist / Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** In a 2020 article, Piper reflected on Psalm 112:7–8 as supremely relevant in a year of pandemic, political upheaval, and instability: “The Hebrew word for steady… is actually a passive verb meaning *upheld*.… Steadiness in the Lord is upheldness. It is not mere courage or patience or sobriety, but dependence on the upholder — the all-wise, all-powerful, all-loving King over all.” He draws three paths into upheldness: (1) fearing God drives out other fears; (2) delighting in God's commands produces resilient obedience; (3) the certainty of future triumph makes present affliction bearable. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/more-bad-news-may-come)

---

## Verse 8

**"His heart is assured; he does not fear, until he looks in triumph on his foes."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that “his heart is established” is “almost a repetition of the phrase in v.7, 'his heart is fixed' — seemingly, therefore, superfluous, but really emphasizing the point, which is of great moment.” Hengstenberg also comments on the repetition as emphatic. The Pulpit Commentary links this to 1 John 4:18: “Perfect love casteth out fear.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Clarke: “‘His heart is propped up;’ he is buttressed up by the strength of his Maker.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

Spurgeon: “His love to God is deep and true, his confidence in God is firm and unmoved; his courage has a firm foundation, and is supported by Omnipotence. He has become settled by experience, and confirmed by years. He is not a rolling stone, but a pillar in the house of the Lord.” On “until he see his desire upon his enemies,” Spurgeon carefully adds: “Grace makes him desire his enemies' good: though nature leads him to wish to see justice done to his cause, he does not desire for those who injure him anything by way of private revenge.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Gill: “until he sees them all slain and destroyed, as the Israelites saw the Egyptians on the sea shore.” He notes that the supplied phrase “his desire” could simply be “vengeance” (as Psalm 58:10), the punishment of God on the wicked. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

---

## Verse 9

**"He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be lifted high in honor."**

This verse is quoted by Paul in 2 Corinthians 9:9 to encourage Christian generosity. Guzik notes that “dispersed” implies “a wise and thoughtful distribution as part of the discretion that guides his affairs.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

Horne (cited in Guzik): the generosity is not “given indiscriminately and at random, but 'dispersed,' like precious seed, with prudence and discretion, according to the nature of the soil, and in proper season, so as to produce the most plentiful harvest.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

Ellicott: “The conjugation of the verb indicates a frequent and customary action.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary: “There is no virtue in mere 'dispersing,' since spendthrifts 'disperse' even more lavishly than virtuous men. The only laudable 'dispersing' is that which has for its object the relief of distress, and which is wisely directed to that object.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

On **“his horn will be lifted high in honor,”** Clarke says: “His power and authority shall be exalted with honour. He shall rise to influence only through his own worth, and not by extortion or flattery.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/) For the horn image, Ellicott refers to Psalm 75:5. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon closes his exposition of v.9 by observing: “Let it be observed, in summing up the qualities of the God fearing man, that he is described not merely as righteous, but as one bearing the character to which Paul refers in the memorable verse, 'For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.' Kindness, benevolence, and generosity, are essential to the perfect character; to be strictly just is not enough, for God is love, and we must love our neighbour as ourselves.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Barrow (cited in Spurgeon): “When all the flashes of sensual pleasure are quite extinct, when all the flowers of secular glory are withered away… the bountiful man's state will be still firm and flourishing, and 'his righteousness shall endure for ever.'” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

G. Campbell Morgan (cited in Guzik) ties the whole psalm together: “Let it now be read again in close connection with the preceding one [Psalm 111], and it will be seen that the supreme fact about this man is that he has indeed become like the God Whom he fears and obeys. The very things celebrated in the praise of Jehovah are those which constitute the excellencies of this man who fears Him.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

---

## Verse 10

**"The wicked man will see and be grieved; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desires of the wicked will perish."**

The Pulpit Commentary: “The wicked hate the righteous (Psalm 105:25), and are naturally 'grieved' to see them prosper.” The gnashing of teeth recalls Job 16:9, Psalm 35:16, Psalm 37:12, and Acts 7:54. “Civilization represses these emotional displays, but the feeling remains nevertheless.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/112.htm)

Spurgeon is vivid: “The ungodly shall first see the example of the saints to their own condemnation, and shall at last behold the happiness of the godly and to the increase of their eternal misery.” He pictures the wicked man melting “like wax” and “like the snail” that “melts as it proceeds, leaving a slimy trail behind.” The final line — “the desire of the wicked shall perish” — he reads as: “He shall not achieve his purpose, he shall die a disappointed man. By wickedness he hoped to accomplish his purpose — that very wickedness shall be his defeat.” (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps112.cfm)

Gill connects the gnashing of teeth to Luke 13:28, where the wicked weep and gnash their teeth seeing the righteous in the kingdom. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/112.htm)

Trapp (cited in Spurgeon/Guzik): “The covetous wretch who sat a brood upon his bags, and befooled the bountiful man, shall himself come to beggary, which he so much feared, and be ready to eat his own nails through envy at the other's prosperity.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-112/)

---

## Notable Points Across Traditions

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Both read the psalm through a strong Christological and Calvinistic lens. Gill sees the “man” as ultimately Christ, whose spiritual seed are believers. Spurgeon emphasizes that the righteousness that “endures forever” includes the imputed righteousness of Christ. Both also caution against reading the material promises as absolute — they are old-covenant promises fulfilled in a general, not universal, sense.

**Reformed (Ligonier, Hengstenberg, Calvin):** Stress the tension between the psalm's promises and the reality of suffering. Calvin says the righteous are indeed “liable to the incidents common to humanity” but their confidence “remains unshaken.” Ligonier links the enduring righteousness to justification: “Only His perfection can establish us so firmly that we can never be moved from the state of salvation.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/unmovable-righteous)

**Charismatic/Pentecostal (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik reads the material promises more directly, while still noting they are “general” promises, not universal guarantees. He emphasizes that the psalm paints a portrait of the believer that is “partially fulfilled in the godly man or woman, and perfectly fulfilled in the man Jesus Christ.” He also highlights the practical wisdom dimension: the psalm “deals realistically with the temptations that go with the possession of money.”

**Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary):** Both read with close attention to the Hebrew text. Ellicott consistently notes translation nuances (e.g., “mighty” = wealthy; “guide his affairs” = sustain his cause in judgment; “righteousness” = liberality). The Pulpit Commentary reads the adjectives of v.4 as describing the godly man, not God — a point of genuine divergence from Gill and others.

---

## What I Could Not Find

- **Catholic / Orthodox** specific readings (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org): The search tool returned no usable results from these sources.
- **Lutheran** specific readings (lcms.org, 1517.org): No results returned.
- **Methodist / Wesleyan** specific readings (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com): No results returned.
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org): No results returned.
- **Prosperity gospel / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace** readings: No results that discussed Psalm 112 from these perspectives were found.

These gaps mean the notes above represent principally the Baptist, Reformed, Anglican, and broadly evangelical traditions that dominate the accessible sources.
